title: Foreign Investors Return to Indian Equities After Four-Month, $29 Billion Selloff
excerpt: FPIs have invested over ₹15,000 crore in Indian stocks in July, ending a brutal selling streak. Jefferies' Chris Wood and Goldman Sachs say India's valuations are finally looking attractive again.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Foreign portfolio investors invested ₹15,157 crore in Indian equities in July, ending a four-month selloff.
  • FPIs sold a net $21.1 billion in Indian equities in 2026, surpassing last year's record outflow.
  • Goldman Sachs targets Nifty 50 at 26,500 by June 2027, citing attractive valuations.
  • Domestic mutual funds invested ₹50,643 crore in June, providing stability amid foreign outflows.
  • Analysts see potential for further inflows as India's market valuations improve.

  • Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have turned net buyers of Indian equities in July, investing ₹15,157 crore after selling over ₹2.61 lakh crore across the previous four months.
  • Jefferies' Chris Wood says India remains structurally attractive, with foreign investors having sold a net $21.1 billion in 2026 — surpassing last year's record $18.8 billion outflow.
  • Goldman Sachs sees "ample room for flows to return" with Nifty 50 trading below its five-year average valuation, and targets 26,500 by June 2027.

The Reversal

Foreign portfolio investors have returned as net buyers of Indian equities in July, investing ₹15,157 crore and ending a four-month selling streak that had rattled market sentiment across Asia's third-largest economy.

The turnaround follows one of the most brutal stretches of foreign selling in Indian market history. Over the four months from March through June, FPIs pulled out more than ₹2.61 lakh crore from Indian stocks, according to data from the National Securities Depository. The outflows included ₹1.17 lakh crore in March alone — the heaviest single-month selling this year — followed by ₹60,847 crore in April, ₹32,963 crore in May, and ₹49,340 crore in June, according to The Indian Eye.

Cumulatively, foreign investors have sold a net $21.1 billion worth of Indian equities so far in 2026, surpassing last year's record outflow of $18.8 billion, according to data cited in Jefferies' latest GREED & fear report.

> **"Over the four months from March through June, FPIs pulled out more than ₹2.61 lakh crore from Indian stocks, according to data from the National Securities Depository."**

Why Foreigners Sold — and Why They're Coming Back

The selloff was driven largely by a global rotation into AI and semiconductor-linked markets. As the artificial intelligence boom reshaped emerging market allocations, investors aggressively piled into South Korea and Taiwan at India's expense. India's weighting in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index dropped from 19.5% to 11.5% since early 2025, while Korea surged from 9% to 20.6% and Taiwan climbed from 19.7% to 25%.

"Over the four months from March through June, FPIs pulled out more than ₹2.61 lakh crore from Indian stocks, according to data from the National Securities Depository."

"If India has been out of favour as the reverse AI trade, at least it has not been reduced to complete benchmark irrelevance for emerging market investors, which is the real risk now facing ASEAN markets."

— Christopher Wood, Global Head of Equity Strategy, Jefferies

The tide appears to be turning. Analysts attribute the July reversal to improving domestic macroeconomic indicators, a stable rupee, easing global risk sentiment, and valuations that have corrected to more attractive levels. The Nifty MidCap 100 Index has rallied 19.2% from its April low and recently touched a fresh record high, according to Jefferies.

Goldman Sachs Sees Room to Run

Goldman Sachs, in its July 11 "India Strategy: Room To Rebound" report, said India's outlook has improved in recent weeks amid lower commodity prices, a stabilized currency, and healthy second-quarter earnings expectations. The brokerage noted that foreign positioning in Indian equities remains "ultra-light," creating substantial scope for further inflows.

Goldman expects the Nifty 50 to recover toward its June 2027 target of 26,500, implying roughly 10% upside from current levels. Large-cap stocks and banking names, which bore the brunt of foreign selling earlier this year, could benefit most as overseas investors gradually rebuild allocations.

Nifty 50 now trades at a one-year forward multiple of 20.0x, below its five-year average of 21.5x, while MSCI India sits at 21.6x versus a five-year mean of 23.7x, according to Bajaj Broking research cited by Outlook Money.

Domestic Flows Provide a Floor

Even as foreign money fled, domestic institutional investors held the line. Equity-oriented mutual funds deployed ₹50,643 crore into stocks in June, drawing down cash holdings to ₹1.84 lakh crore — the lowest level of 2026, according to Outlook Money. SIP contributions rose 2.7% to ₹31,781 crore in June, approaching March's record of ₹32,087 crore.

Jefferies highlighted that mutual fund inflows totaled $13.4 billion in Q1 2026, with an additional $1.7 billion per month flowing from the National Pension Scheme into equities. This domestic liquidity cushion has helped Indian benchmarks remain resilient despite the foreign exodus.

What to Watch

For investors tracking Indian markets from abroad, the sustainability of the FPI reversal will depend on several factors: the trajectory of Q1 FY27 corporate earnings, geopolitical stability — particularly the US-Iran situation — and whether the global AI trade begins to rotate. If the semiconductor-heavy concentration in emerging market indices starts to unwind, India's diversified earnings profile could attract significant reallocation.

Both Sensex and Nifty 50 remain 8-10% below their year-to-date highs, but with institutional confidence strengthening on both the domestic and foreign fronts, the market's risk-reward profile is shifting.
